Covid19: the Search for a Silver Bullet.

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is an effective and safe Covid19 treatment any closer within reach, or is our desperation fueling unwarranted optimism?

Unique Selling Point:
We speak to two of South Africa's leading infectious disease experts for insights into the global search for a possible Covid19 treatment, a scientific undertaking spanning more than 500 medical trials involving thousands of volunteers. We also hear from a company harnessing the power of AI to radically speed-up a process that would otherwise take years. And, throughout, we ask: are we discarding scientific rigour in this race against time?

Summary:
There are - at last count - more than 500 clinical trials and research studies underway around the world as part of a desperate search for a possible treatment or cure for Covid19. It's important work because a vaccine - even by the most optimistic estimates - is more than a year away. That's creating significant anxiety because it means the next 12, 18 or possibly 24 months of our lives will be characterised by social distancing and - in the event of a transmissions spike - periods of lock-down.

A treatment - or even a cure - would clearly make that a less frightening proposition. the term "game-changer" is overused but, with case fatality rates currently hovering at anywhere between 1 and 10%, anything that makes admission to hospital routine rather than a medical emergency would be deserving of the title.

That's why so many people are working so hard to find a new or existing drug that could do precisely that. Trials are already underway and many more are planned and, in some cases, early results are already being published. With luck, one or perhaps several will prove effective and the gap between now and a vaccine will seem a little less daunting.

But, there are caveats: there's no guarantee a treatment or cure will be found nor is it a sure thing an effective drug will be safe at the required dosage and there's always the danger that scientific rigour falls by the wayside in the quest for speed.

We'll talk to two South African experts about the trials process, the most publicised candidates, the pitfalls and the broader context of the search for a vaccine. We'll canvass them, too, for their views on the ethical dilemmas.

We'll also talk to one of several companies using AI to identify existing drugs and compounds that might help in the fight against the pandemic.

VO: There are currently about a hundred and 20 vaccines being researched in various countries. Some – like this one at the university of Oxford - are already being tested on humans. But, a successful candidate – if we get one – is still a year away, probably more.
Link: Which is why I’m sitting at a desk in the middle of a farm track: if the wait’s going to be that long it’s probably a good idea to embrace a different way of doing things. And, if we’ve learned anything, it’s that there’s nothing normal about the new normal.

But I think everyone should really consider (CUT) that they're going to be at risk and they need to have a fundamental change in how they think about lifestyle as we go forward in the next few months.

But, there are caveats: there's no guarantee a treatment or cure will be found nor is it a sure thing an effective drug will be safe at the required dosage and there's always the danger that scientific rigour falls by the wayside in the quest for speed. We'll talk to two South African experts about the trials process, the most publicised candidates, the pitfalls and the broader context of the search for a vaccine. We'll canvass them, too, for their views on the ethical dilemmas. We'll also talk to one of several companies using AI to identify existing drugs and compounds that might help in the fight against the pandemic.
